newsitem.title: NORTH KOREA: Foreign investment deals may be clinched at N.Korean meet.
newsitem.headline: Foreign investment deals may be clinched at N.Korean meet.

text.p: Reclusive North Korea's biggest experiment with capitalism moved into high gear on Sunday as foreign businessmen scurried to clinch agreements or lay the groundwork for deals in the isolated Stalinist state.
Speculation mounted that pacts worth hundreds of millions of dollars could be announced when a historic three-day investment forum concluded with a late afternoon news conference.

North Korea, which has sneered at the capitalist world for decades, is now hoping to create a 750 sq km (280 sq mile) free trade zone in its northeast and attract enough foreign investors to help revive its teetering economy.

Chinese and overseas Koreans are expected to provide much of the US$100 million required to make the Rajin-Sonbong free trade zone a success in the short term and could be among the first foreign businessmen to announce deals.

Observers at the forum said negotiations for a joint venture flour mill with the bordering Chinese province of Yangi and talks on construction of an oil refinery were the most likely to yield the first deals.
Yangi province was also said to be discussing a deal for a bottling plant and an plastic factory, while Hong Kong and overseas Korean concerns were focusing on a five-star hotel.
The Japanese city of Niigata and China's Jilin province were also poised on Sunday to sign an agreement to provide some level of infrastructure support for the zone, officials said.
"There are definitely things happening here, it's just a matter of what people do after the forum rather than what they say here," said an economic researcher from the United States.

North Korea's first attempt at linking up with capitalism has attracted 550 businessmen and reporters who joined North Korean officials for seminars on tourism, banking, agriculture, electronics manufacturing and infrastructure development.
North Korea, eager to impress its guests, built a gleaming new conference centre in the middle of the free trade zone on the Tumen River border region with China and Russia.

North Korean officials quickly got down to business. With the paint still wet on the new building, the chairman of the counrty's Committee for Promotion of External Economic Coooperation appealed for billions of dollars of investment.
Kim Jong-u painted a picture of a free trade zone with low taxes, visa-free travel, high-tech infrastructure and laws governing investment.

Lectures during the weekend included case studies of the handful of joint ventures already under way as well as discussions about how to work with a North Korean government that has long held capitalists in contempt.
Small conference rooms on the second floor of the centre were available for private meetings, and many were occupied throughout the weekend.
North Korean officials were seen nervously puffing cigarettes as their foreign counterparts listened to their words through inexperienced translators.

The omnipresent "guides" shadowing guests eventually relaxed enough to allow foreigners to walk freely in Rajin and Sonbong cities. Businessmen and researchers were seen wandering into residential neighborhoods, much to the surprise of residents.
Outside urban areas, Rajin-Songong appeared desolate, with only one village visible on the 50 km (30 mile) drive to the Chinese border to the north.

During the hour-long journey, visitors saw only two cargo trucks on the road which serves as an overland shipping route for goods from Ragjin Sonbong to Yangi Province. The goods originate in Pusan, South Korea, with which North Korea is still technically at war, and are brought to Ragjin Sonbong by boat.
On the North Korean side of Wonjong Bridge, the only link to China over the Tumen River, a few guards monitored border traffic and checked visas and identifications.
Traffic was light. Trucks and buses carrying Chinese tourists crossed about every thirty minutes.
